subject: Creating a mesh in higher dimensions

messages.author: f8d15de6c9343d76
messages.subject: Creating a mesh in higher dimensions
parts:
Hi All,

I'm an INLA newbie, and could use some help trying to create an SPDE model for high-dimension data.  All of the examples I've seen have been strictly 2D spatial models, however the problem I'm working on needs a minimum of 5, possibly 7 dimensions in the spatial analysis.

A toy example is trying to build a mesh over a combination of position and velocity:

n = 1000
x = rnorm(n)
y = rnorm(n)
z = rnorm(n)
vx = rnorm(n)
vy = rnorm(n)
vz = rnorm(n)
mesh.6d <- inla.mesh.create(cbind(x,y,z,vx,vy,vz))

This fails with the error:
fmesher.cc(567) Points not in the plane or on a sphere, and triangulation empty.
meshc.cc(1359)  NOT IMPLEMENTED: bool fmesh::MeshC::CET(int, double)

I've been unable to find examples or documentation for building models in higher dimensions, so I don't know what options are available.  Does anyone have experience building SPDE models in dimension >3?

Best,
Jason Bates

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Creating a mesh in higher dimensions
parts:
Hi Jason,

the fmesher code only supports 2-manifolds (and the R code also
supports 1-manifolds).
There is 3-manifold support with tetrahedral meshes in the
experimental https://github.com/finnlindgren/inlamesh3d package.
There, the package requires the user to create the mesh themselves,
e.g. using delaunayn on a suitable set of points, and the package then
has inla.mesh.fem and inla.spde.make.A methods to work with such
tetrahedral meshes.

In theory, that code could be extended to dim > 3, but the gain of
using sparse FEM representations of the field diminishes with higher
dimensions.

In your 6-dimensional case, one could consider a tensor product basis
between two tetrahedral meshes; one for location and one for velocity;
it should be straightforward to construct such a model with precision
kronecker products and inla.generic(), but I suspect the computational
cost wouldn't be worth it. If you do try it, I strongly recommend
_not_ using observed locations as seed points for the mesh; consider a
quasi-regular set of points instead, and rely on inla.spde.make.A to
make the link between basis functions and observation locations.
Data-seeded irregular meshes can be computationally deficient, leading
to singular matrices etc (which is why the "cutoff" argument to
inla.spde.2d() exists, to prevent direct use of arbitrarily close
points).

Finn
